question: The Campania Region has granted permission for the construction of a plant to process domestic and industrial sludge, and to produce fertilising compost and dried sludge for energy recovery purposes, in the area of Agro di Savignano Irpino, which is in the province of Avellino, but on the regional border with Apulia. The plant may have environmental repercussions for the Cervaro stream basin.

The Cervaro stream valley is a Natura 2000 site and, given the intrinsic nature of the potential plant and its location, but also in the context of accidents, it is clear that the plant could affect the local environment. Nor was the impact assessment concerning environmental effects for the Valle del Cervaro Natura 2000 site taken into account.
In the light of the Habitats Directive (Directive 92/43/EEC), which was adopted to promote the maintenance of biodiversity and introduced the Natura 2000 Europe-wide network of protected areas: 1.
Can the Commission ask the Campania Region to provide justification for why, in breach of the Habitats Directive, it has given the green light to the aforementioned plans?
What steps will the Commission take vis-a-vis the Italian authorities to protect Natura 2000 sites?
answer: The Commission has no specific information about the project referred to by the Honourable Member. According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (1), any plan or project that is likely to have a significant impact on a Natura 2000 site must be subject to an assessment of its impacts in view of the site's conservation objectives.

In the light of the conclusions of the assessment, the competent national authorities shall agree to the plan or project only after having ascertained that it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned. In the case of a negative assessment, national authorities may authorise the project only for imperative reasons of overriding public interest and provided that there are no alternative solutions.

In such cases, Member States shall take compensatory measures to ensure that the overall coherence of Natura 2000 is protected. The Commission published several guidance documents to help Member States implement the above-mentioned provisions (2).

Italy has transposed these provisions in its national legislation (3) and, in 2019, adopted tailored national guidelines to facilitate and ensure their consistent implementation across its regions (4). The Region of Campania has also adopted relevant and up-todate rules transposing the above provisions and guidelines (5).

Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules, and to take the necessary steps for enforcement. In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission will continue monitoring the situation and may decide to take appropriate action.
In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action (6), the Commission focuses on systemic noncompliance.
